questions.concept: Wayfinding to designated pickup zones at crowded venues
questions.question: You're the PM for a ride-hailing app. After concerts at a large stadium, riders and drivers keep failing to find each other: pickups take 15+ minutes and many trips are cancelled. GPS is accurate to about 30 metres in the crowd. What's the best product change?
options: Show a larger map pin and a live photo of the driver's car to help riders find it
Route all post-event pickups to a few numbered pickup zones, guide riders there on foot, and match them to drivers at that zone
Let riders and drivers call each other in one tap from the trip screen
Improve GPS accuracy with better location fusion so riders and drivers see each other's exact position
rationales: Better visual cues help in the last few metres, but the failure here starts earlier: riders and cars are in different places entirely.
Correct: it changes the system, not just the signal. Fixed zones make the meeting point unambiguous and let you manage supply at each zone.
Calls help one pair at a time but don't scale in a noisy crowd, and they still leave both sides negotiating a spot.
Even perfect GPS doesn't help when a car can't stop where the rider is standing. Crowds and blocked roads, not accuracy, are the constraint.
questions.explanation: The root problem isn't location precision; it's thousands of people and cars converging on undefined spots in a dense, chaotic space. Turning a fuzzy meeting point into a fixed, signed place (a numbered zone) removes the coordination problem for both sides. Matching at the zone also lets you queue cars and riders, which cuts circling and cancellations.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who notice when a problem is about coordination between two sides, not one user's UI. Naming the real constraint (crowds and road access) before solving signals strong product sense.

questions.concept: Proactive order-status updates to prevent 'where is my order' contacts
questions.question: An Indian D2C skincare brand sells mainly through its website and gets 40% of its support chats asking 'where is my order?'. Shipping times are normal. What should the PM do first?
options: Hire more support agents during peak hours to answer order-status chats faster
Put a clearer 'Track order' link in the website footer and the confirmation email
Send proactive WhatsApp updates at key shipping milestones, including delays, with a tracking link
Add a chatbot that looks up order status when customers ask for it
rationales: This treats the symptom at a higher cost. Contacts stay just as frequent; they are simply answered faster.
Helpful, but it still depends on customers looking for the link. Many won't, especially on mobile.
Correct: proactive updates remove the uncertainty that causes the contact, and WhatsApp is where Indian shoppers actually see messages.
Automation lowers the cost per contact, but customers still have to reach out, so the anxiety and volume remain.
questions.explanation: Customers ask 'where is my order?' because they're anxious and don't know what's happening. The cheapest contact is the one that never happens: pushing updates at moments that matter (shipped, out for delivery, delayed) in the channel they already read answers the question before it's asked. Pull-based fixes still make the customer do the work.
questions.interview_tip: When a support driver is a 'status' question, strong candidates move from answering faster to preventing the question. Mention the channel your users actually check.

questions.concept: Assisted commerce via local agents for users who won't transact alone
questions.question: You're building an e-commerce app for small towns in India. Research shows many target users want branded goods but don't trust paying online, struggle with English product pages, and rarely install new apps. Which approach best fits this segment?
options: Work through trusted local assistants, such as shop owners, who browse and order for customers and accept cash on their behalf
Translate the full app into regional languages and run a big app-install campaign in small towns
Build a voice assistant inside the app so users can search by speaking in their language
Offer large first-order discounts to get users over the trust barrier with online payment
rationales: Correct: borrowing an existing trust relationship solves trust, language and app adoption together. It's how many rural-commerce models have scaled.
Translation fixes language, but users still need to install the app and trust online payment. The campaign fights the 'rarely install apps' barrier head-on.
Voice helps with language and literacy, but it still lives inside an app users haven't installed and still asks them to pay online.
Discounts can create a one-off trial but don't build lasting trust. Users who distrust paying online won't stay because of a coupon.
questions.explanation: This segment has three barriers at once: trust, language and app adoption. A person they already know and trust (an assisted-commerce agent) removes all three in one move: the agent handles the app, the language and the payment. Fixing one barrier at a time inside the app still requires users to install and trust it first.
questions.interview_tip: In product sense rounds, list all the barriers a segment faces and look for one solution that removes several at once. That shows you're designing for the real user, not a generic one.

questions.concept: Snooze as a middle option between act and dismiss
questions.question: Users of a to-do app often dismiss reminders they can't act on right now, then forget the task. What's the simplest fix?
options: Show the reminder in red to signal that the task is urgent
Add a 'snooze' option so users can push the reminder to a later time
Stop letting users dismiss reminders until the task is completed
Send the same reminder again every 15 minutes until the task is done
rationales: Colour doesn't change the problem: the user still can't act now and still has no way to defer.
Correct: it gives users the choice they actually need and keeps the task alive without nagging.
Blocking dismiss is frustrating and pushes users to turn off notifications entirely.
Repeating the reminder creates alert fatigue and makes users more likely to mute the app.
questions.explanation: When the only choices are 'do it now' or 'dismiss', users who can't act now pick dismiss and lose the task. A snooze matches what they actually want: 'remind me later'. Giving a middle option fits the real situation instead of forcing a false choice.
questions.interview_tip: Watch for designs that force users into a false choice. Spotting the missing option is a quick, concrete win in product sense answers.

questions.concept: Inbox placement drop at one email provider behind falling reactivation
questions.question: A subscription app's email win-back campaign reactivates 30% fewer lapsed users this month. Email volume and content haven't changed. Open rates fell sharply for Gmail users but not for other providers. What's the most likely cause to check first?
options: Gmail began routing the emails to spam or Promotions, so fewer users ever saw them
A bug in the app is stopping users from reactivating after they click
Lapsed users this month are less interested in the product than last month's
The win-back offer is less attractive than competitors' current offers
rationales: Correct: a change limited to one provider, with nothing else changed, is the classic sign of a deliverability problem.
A post-click bug would lower conversion after opens, but here the opens themselves fell, and only for Gmail.
A drop in user interest would show up across all providers, not just Gmail.
Competitor offers would affect everyone. They don't explain why only Gmail opens fell.
questions.explanation: The drop is isolated to one email provider while content and volume are unchanged. That points to delivery, not demand: if Gmail's filters started placing the emails in spam or Promotions, those users simply didn't see them. Checking inbox placement and sender reputation for Gmail is the fastest way to confirm.
questions.interview_tip: In root-cause questions, the segment where the drop shows up is your best clue. Saying 'it's only one provider, so check delivery before demand' shows structured thinking.

questions.concept: North Star for a B2B recruiting platform
questions.question: You're the PM for a B2B recruiting platform that companies pay to find and hire candidates. Which is the best North Star metric?
options: Number of candidate profiles in the database
Number of messages recruiters send to candidates
Number of hires made through the platform each month
Number of job postings created each month
rationales: Database size is a supply metric that can grow with low-quality or stale profiles.
Messages can be spammy. More outreach can even mean the matching is getting worse.
Correct: hires reflect delivered value for employers and candidates, and they tend to drive renewals.
Postings show demand, not success. A company can post many jobs and fill none.
questions.explanation: A North Star should capture the core value customers get. Companies pay a recruiting platform to fill roles, so a hire made through the platform is the moment of real value. Postings, profiles and messages are inputs that can grow without anyone getting hired.
questions.interview_tip: Anchor a North Star on the moment the customer gets value, then name the inputs that drive it. Interviewers look for that link between value and metric.

questions.concept: Purchase frequency calculation
questions.question: An online store had 12,000 orders from 4,000 unique customers last quarter. What is the purchase frequency for the quarter?
options: 0.33 orders per customer
3 orders per customer
4,000 customers
12,000 orders
rationales: This is the ratio flipped (customers per order), which isn't a meaningful frequency measure.
Correct: 12,000 orders ÷ 4,000 customers = 3 orders per customer.
This is the customer count, not how often each customer buys.
This is just the total order count; it doesn't account for how many customers placed them.
questions.explanation: Purchase frequency is total orders divided by unique customers: 12,000 / 4,000 = 3. It tells you how often the average customer buys in the period, and together with average order value it drives revenue per customer.
questions.interview_tip: Simple metric definitions come up as warm-ups. Say the formula out loud and what decision it informs.

questions.concept: Measuring a safety feature by harm-rate reduction, not feature usage
questions.question: A dating app launches a feature that warns users before they share their phone number with a new match. What's the best primary success metric?
options: Number of times the warning is shown each week
Reports of scams or harassment per 1,000 new matches, compared with a control group
Percentage of users who tap 'Got it' on the warning
Number of users who mention the feature in app-store reviews
rationales: Impressions measure exposure. A warning shown often but ignored doesn't make anyone safer.
Correct: it measures the outcome the feature is meant to change, normalised and compared with a control.
Tapping 'Got it' mostly measures dismissal. Users can acknowledge the warning and still share their number.
Review mentions are rare, biased and say nothing about whether harm went down.
questions.explanation: A safety feature exists to reduce harm, so success means less harm, not more usage. Measuring scam or harassment reports normalised by exposure (per 1,000 matches) against a control shows whether the warning actually changes outcomes. Impressions and taps only show that people saw it.
questions.interview_tip: For trust and safety features, interviewers want you to measure harm prevented rather than engagement. Say 'success here means fewer bad outcomes'.

questions.concept: Deliberate slowdown experiments to price the value of latency
questions.question: Engineering wants a quarter to make your shopping app's search 200 ms faster. Leadership asks how much revenue that would bring. What's the best way to estimate it before building?
options: Use the figure from a well-known study of another company's speed gains
Survey users about how much they would value faster search
Run a test that adds 200 ms of delay for a small random group and measure the revenue drop
Compare revenue between users on fast and slow phones in last month's data
rationales: Other companies have different users and baselines. It's a useful prior but not evidence for your app.
Users can't reliably say how much 200 ms matters to them; stated preferences don't predict behaviour well here.
Correct: a randomised slowdown gives a causal, product-specific estimate of what latency is worth, before any build.
Phone speed is linked to income and region, so the comparison mixes speed with who the users are.
questions.explanation: You can't test a speed-up you haven't built, but you can test the opposite: slow things down a little for a random group. Because it's randomised, the revenue loss is a causal estimate of how much latency matters in your product, which you can use to estimate the value of a speed-up of similar size. Keep the group small and the test short, since it costs some revenue.
questions.interview_tip: Mentioning slowdown experiments shows you know how to measure something you can't build yet. Also note the cost of the test and how you'd limit it.

questions.concept: Randomisation balances unobserved confounders
questions.question: Why do teams randomly assign users to control and treatment, instead of letting users opt in to the new feature and comparing them?
options: Random assignment makes the test finish faster than an opt-in comparison
Random assignment guarantees the new feature will show a positive result
Random assignment means you don't need to check statistical significance
Random assignment makes the groups alike on average, including traits you can't measure
rationales: Speed depends on traffic and effect size, not on whether assignment is random.
Randomisation makes results fair, not favourable. The feature can still lose.
You still need significance testing; randomisation only makes the comparison valid.
Correct: randomisation removes selection bias by balancing both measured and unmeasured traits.
questions.explanation: Users who opt in are different: often more engaged or more curious. Any difference you see could come from who they are, not from the feature. Random assignment spreads those traits evenly across groups, including ones you can't see, so a difference between groups can be credited to the feature.
questions.interview_tip: A crisp one-line reason for randomisation is expected in any experimentation round. Use the word 'confounders' and give an example like engaged users opting in.

questions.concept: CCTV retention storage for a retail chain
questions.question: A retail chain has 500 stores, each with 8 cameras recording 24/7 at about 1 Mbps. It must keep 30 days of footage. Roughly how much storage does it need?
options: About 1.3 petabytes
About 13 terabytes
About 13 petabytes
About 130 terabytes
rationales: Correct: 4,000 cameras × 10.8 GB/day × 30 days ≈ 1.3 PB.
This is 100 times too small, a common result of mixing up megabits and megabytes and dropping a zero.
This is 10 times too large, as if each camera recorded at 10 Mbps.
This is 10 times too small; it's roughly what you'd get if you used 3 days instead of 30.
questions.explanation: 1 Mbps is 0.125 MB per second. Over a day (86,400 seconds) that's about 10.8 GB per camera. The chain has 500 × 8 = 4,000 cameras, so about 43 TB per day. Over 30 days that's about 1,300 TB, or roughly 1.3 PB. Compression and motion-only recording could cut this, which is a good follow-up point.
questions.interview_tip: In storage estimates, interviewers watch for bits vs bytes and unit conversions. State each step and round sensibly, then mention what could reduce the number.

questions.concept: Annual LED bulb unit sales in India
questions.question: Roughly how many LED bulbs are sold in India each year? Assume about 300 million households, about 6 light points per home, bulbs lasting about 3 years, and some extra demand from shops and offices.
options: About 7 billion
About 700 million
About 7 million
About 70 million
rationales: This is 10 times too large; it would mean replacing every bulb several times a year.
Correct: 1.8 billion points ÷ 3 years ≈ 600 million, plus commercial demand ≈ 700 million.
This is 100 times too small and ignores most of the installed base.
This is 10 times too small, as if each home had less than one bulb.
questions.explanation: Homes: 300 million × 6 = 1.8 billion light points. If each bulb lasts about 3 years, about 600 million are replaced each year. Adding some demand from shops, offices and new homes brings it to roughly 700 million. The method is a replacement-cycle estimate: installed base divided by life span.
questions.interview_tip: For durable goods, the replacement-cycle method (installed base ÷ life span) is the go-to structure. Say your assumptions clearly and do a quick sanity check.

questions.concept: When first-mover advantage is real: pre-empting scarce assets
questions.question: In which situation is being first to market most likely to give a lasting advantage?
options: When the first mover spends heavily to teach customers about a new category
When the first mover can lock up a scarce resource, like the best retail locations or exclusive supply deals
When the product is easy to copy and customers can switch freely
When the technology is changing fast and early versions will soon be outdated
rationales: Educating the market is expensive and helps followers too, who benefit without paying for it.
Correct: scarce assets can't be duplicated by followers, so the early lead becomes lasting.
Easy copying and free switching let followers catch up quickly; being first gives little protection.
Fast-changing technology often favours followers, who can skip the first mover's outdated choices.
questions.explanation: Being first only matters if it lets you get something later entrants can't. Pre-empting scarce assets (prime locations, spectrum, exclusive contracts) is one of the clearest cases. Without a scarce asset, switching costs or network effects, followers can copy and often learn from the first mover's mistakes.
questions.interview_tip: Avoid saying 'first-mover advantage' as if it's automatic. Strong candidates name the specific mechanism that makes being early pay off.

questions.concept: Joint venture entry with a local partner in a regulated market
questions.question: A US digital insurance startup wants to enter a country where insurance needs a local licence, regulators prefer local ownership, and distribution runs through bank branches. Getting a licence alone would take 3+ years. What's the best entry strategy?
options: Apply for its own licence and build a direct-to-consumer app in the meantime to build brand awareness
Acquire a large local insurer outright to get the licence and branches immediately
Launch without a licence as a 'tech platform' and work out compliance once it has users
Form a joint venture with a licensed local insurer or bank that brings the licence and distribution, while the startup brings product and technology
rationales: Going it alone means years without revenue, and a consumer app can't sell insurance without a licence anyway.
A full acquisition is very expensive for a startup and may face the same local-ownership concerns from regulators.
Operating without a licence in a regulated industry risks being shut down and damages trust with regulators for good.
Correct: it gets the licence, the local ownership regulators want, and distribution, while keeping the startup's edge in product.
questions.explanation: In this market, the scarce assets are the licence, regulatory goodwill and bank distribution, and a local partner already has all three. A joint venture lets each side bring what it's good at and gets the startup to market years earlier. The trade-off is sharing control and profits, which is often worth it in regulated markets.
questions.interview_tip: For market-entry questions, identify what the local market's gatekeepers are (licences, distribution, trust) and choose the entry mode that secures them. Mention the trade-off you accept.

questions.concept: Treating free-tier users' cost as a marketing expense
questions.question: A freemium SaaS company spends $2 per month serving each free user. 4% of free users upgrade to a paid plan. How should a PM think about the cost of free users?
options: As irrelevant, because free users don't generate revenue
As a customer acquisition cost, judged by how many free users become paying customers
As a fixed cost that doesn't change as the free tier grows
As a waste that should be cut by removing the free tier entirely
rationales: Free users cost real money to serve, so ignoring them hides an important part of the business's economics.
Correct: framing free users as acquisition spend lets you compare the free tier with other channels using CAC and LTV.
Serving costs grow with the number of free users, so they are variable, not fixed.
Cutting the free tier may cut your best acquisition channel. Decide based on the numbers, not by default.
questions.explanation: In freemium, the free tier is a marketing channel: you pay to serve free users so that some of them upgrade. That makes the cost of free users part of CAC. At $2 a month and a 4% conversion rate, you spend about $50 of free-user cost per paying customer per month of free use, which you can compare with other channels and with LTV.
questions.interview_tip: Showing that you treat a free tier as a channel with its own CAC signals business fluency. Back it with a quick calculation.

questions.concept: Sequencing a regulatory deadline ahead of revenue work
questions.question: Your payments team has two big items next quarter: a new feature sales expects to add $2M in revenue, and changes needed to meet a new regulation that takes effect in 4 months. You can't fit both. What should you do?
options: Do the regulatory work first, since missing the deadline risks fines or losing the right to operate, and plan the revenue feature right after
Split the team in half and work on both at once so neither is fully delayed
Ask legal whether the regulation really applies before committing to anything
Do the revenue feature first, since $2M is a clear business gain and regulators often extend deadlines
rationales: Correct: it treats the deadline as the hard constraint it is and still gives sales a clear plan for the feature.
Splitting the team usually means both are late, including the one with a legal deadline.
Checking scope with legal is sensible, but it shouldn't hold up planning; you'd confirm it in parallel.
Betting on an extension is risky. If it doesn't come, the cost of non-compliance can be far bigger than $2M.
questions.explanation: A regulatory deadline is a hard constraint with a downside that can be much larger than any one feature: fines, blocked transactions, or losing a licence. Revenue features can usually slip a quarter. Sequencing compliance first, then committing a date for the revenue feature and telling sales early, protects the business.
questions.interview_tip: When prioritising, call out hard constraints (legal, security, contracts) separately from value-based trade-offs. Then explain how you'd tell the affected stakeholders.

questions.concept: Purpose of a sprint review
questions.question: At the end of a sprint, your team demos finished work to the sales lead and two customers. Which Scrum event is this, and what is it for?
options: The sprint review: to show stakeholders what was built and get their feedback to shape the backlog
The sprint retrospective: to discuss how the team worked together and what to improve
Sprint planning: to estimate the stories for the next sprint
The daily stand-up: to check each engineer's individual progress
rationales: Correct: the review inspects the work done and adapts the backlog with stakeholder input.
That describes the sprint retrospective, which is about process, not the product.
Estimation happens in backlog refinement and sprint planning, not in the review.
Scrum focuses on the team's outcome, not on checking individuals' output.
questions.explanation: The sprint review looks at the product: the team shows what it built, stakeholders react, and the backlog is updated based on what was learned. It's different from the retrospective, which looks at the team's process.
questions.interview_tip: Knowing the difference between review (the product) and retro (the process) is a quick credibility signal when discussing how you run agile teams.

questions.concept: Single intake channel for cross-team feature requests
questions.question: Your team gets feature requests through Slack DMs, hallway chats, sales emails and support tickets. Requests get lost, and stakeholders feel ignored. What's the best first fix?
options: Set up one intake form or queue for all requests, with a regular triage and a visible status for each
Stop taking ad-hoc requests and only consider items from quarterly planning
Reply to every request right away with an estimate so people feel heard
Tell stakeholders to send requests only to your manager, who will decide what matters
rationales: Correct: one channel plus triage and visible status fixes both lost requests and stakeholders feeling ignored.
Refusing ad-hoc input makes stakeholders feel even more ignored and can miss urgent needs.
Instant estimates without triage create commitments you can't keep and don't stop requests from getting lost.
This moves the bottleneck to your manager and takes away your ownership of the backlog.
questions.explanation: Requests get lost because they come in through too many channels and there's no shared view of them. One front door with a regular triage gives every request a home, lets you compare them side by side, and lets requesters see what happened. That solves both problems: nothing is lost, and people know where they stand.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like mechanisms over heroics. A simple process that scales, like one intake and a triage rhythm, shows you can manage stakeholders as the team grows.

questions.concept: Driving adoption of a new team process through a pilot, not a mandate
questions.question: You think your org should replace long status meetings with short written updates. Several senior engineers are sceptical and say 'we tried that before and nobody read them'. You have no authority over their teams. What's the best approach?
options: Drop the idea, since the engineers already tried it and know it doesn't work
Ask your director to make written updates mandatory across the org from next week
Keep the meetings but send written updates as well, so people can choose
Pilot written updates with your own team for a month, measure time saved and decisions made, and share the results and what you changed from last time
rationales: Past failure is useful information, not a final verdict. Understanding why it failed is the point.
A top-down mandate may get compliance but not buy-in, and it ignores the real lesson from the last attempt.
Doing both adds work for everyone and doesn't test whether written updates can replace the meetings.
Correct: it influences through evidence, takes the sceptics' history seriously, and keeps the risk inside your own team.
questions.explanation: Without authority, evidence and a good example persuade better than mandates. A pilot inside your own scope shows whether the idea works here, answers the 'we tried it before' concern by learning why it failed then, and gives sceptics data instead of opinions. If it works, other teams can adopt it by choice, which tends to last longer.
questions.interview_tip: For 'influence without authority' stories, show a small proof point, respect for the sceptics' concerns, and voluntary adoption. Interviewers want to see how you change minds, not just get approval.

questions.concept: Halting a growth tactic that violates a partner platform's terms
questions.question: Your growth team's best channel automatically messages people through a large social platform. It drives 30% of new signups. You discover it breaks that platform's terms of service, though nobody has complained yet. What do you do?
options: Reduce the message volume so the platform is less likely to notice
Keep running it quietly while you build other channels, then switch it off once they're ready
Raise it with your manager and legal now, plan to stop the tactic, and start shifting effort to compliant channels
Leave it alone, since enforcing the terms is the platform's job, not yours
rationales: Lowering volume to avoid detection is still a violation, just harder to see. It makes the decision worse, not better.
Running it 'until ready' still knowingly breaks the terms, and a ban could hit before the new channels are ready.
Correct: it shows integrity and ownership, involves legal, and pairs stopping the tactic with a plan to replace the growth.
Your company is responsible for how it uses a partner's platform. 'They haven't caught us' isn't a defence.
questions.explanation: Knowingly breaking a partner's terms puts the company at risk of account bans, legal action and reputational damage, and the longer it runs the bigger that risk gets. Ownership means raising it quickly with the right people, even though it hurts your metrics, and having a plan to replace the channel. Strong candidates accept the short-term cost openly.
questions.interview_tip: In ethics-flavoured behavioural questions, interviewers check whether you'll accept a hit to your own metrics to do the right thing. Show who you'd involve and how you'd soften the business impact.

questions.concept: Renegotiating your own commitments when overloaded
questions.question: You've said yes to too much: a launch, two partner integrations and a planning doc are all due in the same two weeks. You can't do all of them well. What's the strongest move?
options: Rank them by impact, tell the affected stakeholders early which items will slip or shrink, and agree new dates with them
Quietly let the lowest-priority item slip and explain only if someone asks
Deliver all four on time at lower quality, since meeting dates builds trust
Work nights and weekends to deliver everything on time without telling anyone
rationales: Correct: it makes clear trade-offs and gives people time to adjust their own plans.
Silent slips surprise people when they find out, which damages trust more than an early heads-up.
Low-quality work on time can cost more trust than a well-explained delay, especially for a launch.
Heroics can work once but aren't sustainable, and they hide the fact that your planning went wrong.
questions.explanation: Overcommitment is common; what matters is how you handle it. Prioritising, then telling stakeholders early and agreeing new plans, keeps trust because nobody is surprised. Heroics and quiet slips both hide the problem until it's too late for others to adjust.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers value people who manage their own capacity openly. Say how you prioritised, who you told, and what you changed to avoid overcommitting again.

questions.concept: Mean opinion score for TTS quality
questions.question: You're choosing a text-to-speech voice for an AI phone agent. Automatic metrics look similar across three vendors. What's the standard way to compare how natural each voice sounds?
options: Compare word error rate when the speech is transcribed back into text
Pick the vendor with the lowest latency, since naturalness is subjective
Compare how many languages each vendor supports
Have a panel of listeners rate samples on a 1–5 scale and compare the mean opinion scores
rationales: Word error rate shows the speech can be understood, but a robotic voice can be perfectly clear.
Latency matters for phone agents, but it doesn't answer the question of which voice sounds most natural.
Language support is a coverage question, not a quality one.
Correct: MOS is the common way to measure how natural or pleasant synthetic speech sounds to people.
questions.explanation: Naturalness is about human perception, so the standard measure is human: a mean opinion score (MOS) where listeners rate samples, usually from 1 to 5. Using the same scripts across vendors and enough listeners makes the comparison fair. Automatic metrics like word error rate check clarity, not whether a voice sounds natural.
questions.interview_tip: For voice AI, show you know which qualities need human judgement and how to measure them fairly: same scripts, enough raters, blind comparison.

questions.concept: Re-validating state before an agent executes a delayed action
questions.question: An AI travel agent plans a trip, then waits for the user to approve before booking. Users often approve hours later, and some bookings fail or charge a different price than shown. What's the best fix?
options: Add a note that prices may change and book whatever price is current
Book immediately when the plan is made and let users cancel if they don't approve
Before executing, re-check price and availability; if anything changed, show the new details and ask again
Shorten the approval window to 10 minutes so the plan is always fresh
rationales: A disclaimer shifts the risk to the user. They approved one price and are charged another, which erodes trust.
Booking before approval removes the user's control and can trigger cancellation fees.
Correct: re-validating right before acting closes the gap between what was approved and what will happen.
A short window reduces the problem but frustrates users and still fails when prices change quickly.
questions.explanation: The agent made its plan using data that went stale while it waited for approval. The safe pattern is to re-check the state of the world just before acting, and if something important changed, go back to the user. That keeps the user's approval tied to what actually happens, which is the point of asking for approval.
questions.interview_tip: For agent design, mention that an approval is only valid for the state it was based on. Spotting stale-state risks shows you think about how agents fail in the real world.

questions.concept: Prompting vs fine-tuning: which changes model weights
questions.question: What is the key difference between prompting a model and fine-tuning it?
options: Neither changes the weights; fine-tuning just stores longer prompts
Prompting changes the model's weights; fine-tuning only changes the input
Both change the model's weights, but fine-tuning does it faster
Fine-tuning changes the model's weights through extra training; prompting only changes the input
rationales: Fine-tuning really does change the weights; it isn't a stored prompt.
This reverses the two. A prompt never changes the model itself.
Prompting doesn't change weights at all, and fine-tuning is usually slower to iterate on.
Correct: fine-tuning updates the weights; prompting works only through the input.
questions.explanation: Prompting guides the model by changing what you send it (instructions, examples, context); the model itself stays the same. Fine-tuning trains the model further on your examples, which changes its weights. That's why prompting is faster and cheaper to change, while fine-tuning can lock in a style or behaviour more reliably.
questions.interview_tip: Being clear on the basics helps when you discuss build choices. Follow up with when you'd pick each: start with prompting, fine-tune when you need consistency at scale.

questions.concept: Explainability requirements for AI in regulated credit decisions
questions.question: A lending app wants to use an LLM to approve or reject small loans from applicants' chat answers. Regulators require lenders to tell rejected applicants the main reasons. What's the best design?
options: Use the LLM to collect and structure information, but make the decision with a rules or scoring model that can give specific reasons
Avoid AI entirely and go back to manual review of every application
Let the LLM decide and ask it to write an explanation for each rejection
Let the LLM decide and give rejected users a general message that the AI found them ineligible
rationales: Correct: it uses the LLM where it adds value and keeps the regulated decision explainable and consistent.
Manual review throws away the benefit. A hybrid can meet the rule and still scale.
A generated explanation can sound plausible without matching the real reasoning, which is risky when regulators ask.
A vague reason likely fails the requirement to tell applicants the main reasons.
questions.explanation: Regulated decisions need reasons that are accurate and consistent. An LLM's after-the-fact explanation may not reflect how it actually decided. Splitting the job, with the LLM for intake and a transparent scoring model for the decision, keeps the user experience benefit while making reasons traceable and auditable.
questions.interview_tip: In regulated AI questions, separate where the model helps from where the decision must be explainable. That shows you can ship AI without creating compliance risk.

questions.concept: Approval fatigue from over-confirming low-risk agent actions
questions.question: Your AI email assistant asks users to confirm every action: archiving, labelling, drafting and sending. Users now approve everything in seconds without reading, including sends. What's the best fix?
options: Add a short required delay before the Approve button becomes clickable
Ask for confirmation twice on every action so users pay more attention
Remove all confirmations, since users approve everything anyway
Let low-risk, reversible actions run without approval, and save confirmations for high-risk ones like sending
rationales: A delay adds friction to every action but doesn't fix the habit; users just wait and click.
More confirmations make the fatigue worse and push users to stop using the assistant.
Removing confirmations for irreversible actions like sending puts users at real risk.
Correct: tiering by risk makes the important confirmations meaningful again.
questions.explanation: When every action needs approval, approvals become a reflex and stop protecting anything, including the risky ones. Matching confirmation to risk lets safe, undoable actions run freely, so the rare confirmation for a send stands out and gets real attention.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who see that too much safety friction can backfire. Tie the level of control to how reversible and costly each action is.

questions.concept: Last-write-wins losing data in offline sync
questions.question: Your notes app works offline and syncs later. When the same note is edited on a phone and a laptop while both are offline, users lose one set of changes. Engineering says sync uses 'last write wins'. What's the right product-level fix?
options: Block editing when the device is offline so conflicts can't happen
Keep last-write-wins but sync more often while devices are online
Always keep the phone's version, since phones are used more often
Merge changes at a finer level, such as per paragraph, and show a conflict copy when edits overlap
rationales: Blocking offline editing removes a core feature to avoid an engineering problem.
Syncing more often doesn't help when both devices are offline, which is when conflicts happen.
Picking one device by rule still silently throws away the other device's changes.
Correct: finer-grained merging keeps most edits, and conflict copies make sure nothing is lost without the user knowing.
questions.explanation: Last-write-wins replaces the whole note with whichever edit arrived last, silently throwing away the other one. Merging at a finer level keeps edits to different parts, and where the same part was changed, keeping a conflict copy lets the user decide instead of losing work. Losing data silently is the outcome to avoid.
questions.interview_tip: Show you understand what a technical choice means for users: 'last write wins' means silent data loss. PMs who translate trade-offs this way work well with engineers.

questions.concept: Foreign keys link related tables
questions.question: In a relational database, an 'orders' table has a 'customer_id' column that points to the 'customers' table. What is 'customer_id' in the orders table called?
options: An index
A view
A foreign key
A primary key
rationales: An index speeds up lookups but doesn't by itself link tables.
A view is a saved query, not a column.
Correct: it references another table's primary key and links the two tables.
The primary key uniquely identifies rows in its own table; in 'orders' that would be order_id.
questions.explanation: A foreign key is a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. Here, each order's customer_id points to one customer, linking the two tables. The database can then enforce that every order belongs to a real customer.
questions.interview_tip: Basic data-modelling terms come up when you write specs or SQL. Using them correctly helps you talk with engineers and analysts.

questions.concept: Win-back discounts training users to churn for deals
questions.question: A streaming app emails a 50% discount to every user who cancels. Win-backs are up, but more users now cancel each month, and many of them come back on the discount. What's happening, and what should you change?
options: Win-backs are working; send the discount sooner, before users cancel
The discount is too small; raise it to 70% so more cancelled users come back
Users have learned that cancelling gets a discount; make offers rarer, targeted by churn reason, and less predictable
Cancellations are rising for an unrelated reason, so keep the win-back offer as it is
rationales: Offering it before cancellation teaches users to threaten to cancel, which has the same problem.
A bigger discount makes the incentive to cancel even stronger and cuts more revenue.
Correct: it names the incentive problem and fixes it with targeting and limits.
Rising cancellations right after a predictable offer is a strong sign the offer is the cause.
questions.explanation: A predictable reward for cancelling teaches users to cancel. Some loyal users now cancel just to get the deal, which raises churn and cuts revenue per user. Targeting offers by churn reason (for example, price-sensitive users only), limiting how often a user can get one, and making them less predictable keeps the win-back benefit without rewarding the behaviour.
questions.interview_tip: Good growth answers check whether a tactic changes user behaviour in bad ways. Mention second-order effects like users gaming an incentive.

questions.concept: Selling speed as a premium tier (Claude Fable 5.2 fast mode, Nov 2026)
questions.question: On November 9, 2026, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, with an optional fast mode that speeds up generation by up to 2.5 times for $16 and $80. As a PM building on it, when does fast mode make the most sense?
options: For overnight batch jobs, since faster generation finishes them sooner
For user-facing features where waiting hurts the experience, like live chat, while background jobs stay on the standard tier
For all traffic, since faster responses always improve every product
Never, since paying double for the same model and answer quality is poor value
rationales: Batch jobs rarely have a user waiting, so the standard tier finishes them well enough at half the price.
Correct: it pays the premium only where latency matters to users and saves money elsewhere.
Doubling cost for traffic where nobody is waiting adds expense without improving anyone's experience.
Speed has real value in interactive features, so ruling it out ignores how latency affects users.
questions.explanation: Fast mode charges twice the standard price for faster generation from the same model. That's worth it only where speed changes outcomes, such as a user waiting in a live chat. For background work nobody watches, the standard tier gives the same quality at half the price. Splitting traffic by how much latency matters is how you get value from a speed tier.
questions.interview_tip: When pricing has tiers by speed or quality, interviewers want you to match each tier to the use cases where it pays off. Citing a recent launch shows you follow the market.
